title: Develop Capabilities
summary: Developing capabilities is the in-house engineering stage of resource development: the adversary identifies a requirement, builds the tool that meets it, and keeps the result exclusive rather than buying or downloading something defenders may already recognise. Outputs range from malware and loaders to exploits, command and control protocols, and self-signed certificates that lend apparent authenticity to a payload. Work may be contracted out, yet it still counts as adversary development when the adversary shapes the requirements and holds exclusive use. From a defender's viewpoint the development itself is largely invisible, so the practical traces appear later as anomalous file features, implausible signing certificates, or code and configuration patterns shared across separate incidents.

beginner.definition: This is when attackers build their own tools instead of buying or downloading them. The tools might be malware, ways to break into software, or fake security certificates. Building your own means fewer people have seen it before, so security products are less likely to recognise it. This work happens long before any victim is attacked. It is preparation, and it takes time, money and skill.
beginner.whyItMatters: Tools that many attackers use are known to security companies, so they are often blocked. A tool written for one campaign has no known signature yet. Custom malware can also be aimed at one type of system or one particular target. Because the code is new, defenders must watch behaviour rather than names. This makes early detection harder and investigation slower. Understanding that attackers build their own tools explains why you cannot rely only on lists of known bad files.
howItWorks: The attacker writes down what the operation needs, such as stealthy access or a specific exploit.
Developers build the tool, sometimes as an in-house team and sometimes as paid contractors.
They test it against common security products before using it in the field.
They may add deliberate clues that point to a different group and mislead investigators.
The tool is then delivered during an operation and updated over time.
Defenders usually meet the tool only after it has already run somewhere.
beginner.example: Think of a locksmith who makes a special key for one building. That key is not sold in shops and no catalogue lists it. A guard who only checks keys against a list of known shapes will wave it through. The locksmith's skill is not the crime. It is the preparation that makes the crime easier. Custom malware is that special key. Because nobody has seen it before, the guard must watch how it is used rather than what it looks like.
takeaways: Attackers can write tools that no security product has seen before.
Behaviour based detection matters as much as signature based detection.
Shared code and settings between incidents can link campaigns together.

objectives: Explain what it means for an adversary to develop capabilities in house.
List the kinds of tooling that fall under this technique.
Describe why custom tooling is harder to detect than known malware.
Recognise that contracted development still counts as adversary capability.
Explain why behaviour based detection complements signature based detection.
